blocks.text: Often called 'the forests of the sea', mangroves are salt-tolerant forests at the meeting of land and sea.

blocks.caption: Profile of the mangrove forest
rows: Sindh (Keti Bandar and Mirpur Sakro in the Indus delta) and the Balochistan coast (Miani Hor, Kalmat Khor, Jiwani and Gawatar Bay)
brackish: fresh river water mixed with salty seawater
oxygen-poor mudflats; trees have breathing roots
Avicennia marina (timmar), about 95% of the forest
crocodiles, shrimps, mudskippers, crabs, lobsters, turtles, snakes, dolphins; flamingo, crane, pelican
threatened by less fresh water from the Indus and by pollution from Karachi; recent restoration projects have helped

blocks.alt: A mangrove scene. Avicennia marina trees with rounded grey-green crowns stand on a mudflat beside a water channel; many pencil-like breathing roots stick up from the mud. Labelled: herons and egrets in the trees, ducks on the water, shrimps under water and crabs on the mud.
blocks.caption: Figure 25.14: A mangrove forest with representative flora and fauna (original drawing after the textbook's painting, Figure 25.14).

blocks.title: Book correction
blocks.text: The printed Figure 25.14 paints stilt (prop) roots, but the book says the forest is 95% Avicennia marina, whose breathing roots are pencil-like pneumatophores rising from the mud; the drawing above shows pneumatophores.
